Messages.Author: pd...@lightlink.com
Messages.Body:
So I was discussing this over in the Disciplinless Bleed Bounce thread,
but figured I'd move it over here, as that thread is getting unweildy.

Anyway, in reference to the idea of disciplinless bleed bounce, I
surmised that such a card wouldn't be such a good idea for various
reasons, and was advocating for different kinds of bleed defense for
non bounce enabled clans/decks. Which got me thinking about the
underutilized bleed reduction idea. Basically, the paradigm of the game
has always been that Auspex gets "good" bleed reduction (assuming for
the discussion that Telepathic Counter is good bleed reduction), and so
non Auspex bleed reduction cards tend to be conditional and mostly low
yeild.

As noted by many previously, Auspex having bleed reduction is, for the
most part, redundant, as if you can use superior Telepathic Counter,
you can also play Telepathic Misdirection, and as bleed bounce is *so*
much better than bleed reduction, Telepathic Counter (and as such,
bleed reduction as a general defense) mostly gets left by the wayside.
Yeah, I realize that occasionally there are situations where Telepathic
Counter is going to make more sense for a deck than Telepathic
Misdirection, but 90% of the time, the deck is just going to use
Telepathic Misdirection instead.

This being the case, why not simply accept that bleed reduction in
Auspex was a bad idea in the first place, and open up bleed reduction
to other disciplines that really could use the help, in terms of bleed
defense? If we simply did away with the idea that Auspex has the choke
hold on good bleed reduction and went from there, a lot of useful cards
could be introduced into the environment and non bounce enabled
clans/decks could gain access to some reasonable reactive bleed defense
without introducing a disciplinless bleed bounce card as a magic
bullet.

There is nothing inherrently "Auspexy" about bleed reduction, such that
it *needs* to be an Auspex power (using Obfuscate to hide resources
your opponents are trying to sabotage; using Animalism to get a swarm
of bugs to foil that robbery against you; using celerity to cut off a
plot before it starts; whatever) and the introduction of other various
(conditional and low yeild) bleed reduction cards indicates that there
is really no need to keep bleed reduction in Auspex. Why not make good,
flexible, bleed reduction cards? Something like an Obfuscate
modifier/reaction card that is +1 stealth/reduce a bleed by 2 (keeping
in mind that this specific example might or might not actually be a
good idea, but the concept stands)? Or a fortitude combat/reaction card
that says prevent 1 damage/reduce a bleed by 2? Something like that,
where there is flexibility (so you don't have to jam your deck up with
possibly unseable bleed defense) and reasonable bleed defense.

The most recent bleed reduction cards (Terra Incognita, Ancestor's
Insight, Confusion of the Eye) have the flexibility part down and are
good cards (Ancestor's Insight is good to the point that I have a
pretty solid deck in current operation that has 18 of them. Yet still
also has a few Telepathich Misdirections...), but still are conditional
and low yeild (i.e. they only ever reduce a bleed by 1, which isn't
really enough to act as solid bleed defense.

This might be a horrible idea. But maybe not. And maybe the key is to
do away with the idea that only Auspex gets good bleed reduction.

-Peter

Messages.Author: pd...@lightlink.com
Messages.Body:
Xian wrote:
> It seems like the design team has been moving that way...I like it.

It has, indicating that they even think it is a good idea (getting more
bleed reduction in play). But I think they have been a bit too stingy
with it--too careful to not introduce a bleed reduction card that makes
Telepathic Counter become wallpapered, as the paradigm always has been
that Auspex gets the good bleed reduction. I think they should just
accept that that is a bad idea (the auspex = good bleed reduction) and
get some solid, non Auspex bleed reduction out there (i.e. not highly
conditional, that reduces a bleed by 2 with a superior discipline, that
has flexibility so it isn't too narrow to actually include in a deck).

Like, Terra Incognita is good as it is flexible (reduce a bleed by 1 or
cancel a bounce at you). Friend of Mine is theoretically good, but as
it is an anarch card and costs a blood, it isn't really that good.
Confusion of the Eye is good, but as the bleed reduction is conditional
and only for 1, it mostly functions as a way to justify putting
Confusion of the Eye in a deck in a general sense for the superior
version, but gives you the ability to cycle and use it if you don' t
need the strong effect of the card--which is good in terms of design,
but not so good in terms of actual bleed defense. Anscestor's Insight
is fantastic (in a narrow group of decks--i.e. Laibon decks with
reliable AUS) due to the flexibility, but then, it is also already in
Auspex. These recent cards are all a good start, but they all (ignoring
Ancestor's Insight) are likely held back by "auspex = good bleed
reduction".

-Peter

Some members of our playgroup was discussing Deflection, and bleed
bounces in general, a week ago and came up with the idea that the
Auspecs bounces are OK, My Enemy's Enemy is probably the most balanced
because you potentially make an enemy at the table that you wouldn't
usually have.

However on the topic of Deflection/Redirection/Telepathic Misdirection
we came up with the idea of instead of bouncing the full bleed you
bounce the bleed -2 but never less than 1.

Our reasoning for this is that you've sent your minion out to undermine
a specific Methuselah's power/influence you get there and everything is
set for a great attack (eg bleed for 5) however when you get there
there is another minion waiting to dominate your mind/saw you coming
and convince you that this is not a good target or it's not the right
place. So yourr minion moves to the new place they've been directed.
However the plan was set up specifically attack the 1st Methuselah's
assets therefore when your minion gets to their new target the attack
isn't as effective. This could equate to a bleed reduciton of 2 but the
attack is always successful to a degree so the bleed cannot be reduced
to less than 1 through bounces. This way bounce does not take over the
game like it currently does.

only some situations, not all of them. Telepathic Counter has one major
advantage over Telepathic Misdirection: it doesn't tap the defender.
This makes it more efficient at defending against more smaller bleeders.
The problem with current TC is, you can't depend on more smaller bleeders.
Sometimes you get one or two mondo bleeders, and then TM is better, all
things considered - including your point about giving your prey a bleed
to occupy his resources. If you up TC to 2/3 however, it covers more
situations better and that should rebalance the choice between the two
more in its favor. Never mind that it's still quite possible to point
at situations where you'd rather be holding a Misdirection than a Counter.
If there weren't situations like that, I'd have obsolesced Telepathic
Misdirection with my hypothesized change. Quite obviously, I wasn't
trying to do that as I made the above point.

> 2 and the acting minion does not untap as normal during its next untap
> phase." That's a card I would play with.

Perhaps. I don't know how far you'd have to go improving Telepathic
Counter to make the two cards seem equally strong, which is a pretty
subject assessment anyway. As I said in my previous post, adding more
strength to the defenders' options doesn't strike me as something that
would make the game better at all. So ultimately, I wouldn't care to make
either adjustment.

IMHO, the real problems of bleed-reduction cards are:

1). You have to leave a vampire untapped (or spend a Wake) to play
them.
2). They become "dead cards" when nobody bleeds you.

Thus, there is no need for making TC stronger - we need a
*disciplineless* card that work for a tapped vampire and can provide
another benefit. Something like this:

Card Name: Elder's Knowledge
Card Type: Action Modifier/Reaction
[Action Modifier] Usable by a vampire if a younger vampire attempted to
block this action or played a reaction card during this action. Draw a
card, then discard a card.
[Reaction] Usable by a vampire (possibly tapped) when a younger vampire
bleeds you. Reduce the bleed by 1.

This card is playable, but not broken. It favors large vampires and
does nothing for weenies. It saves your pool or improves your hand, and
it doesn't require any Disciplines. What else one could expect from a
single card?

Best regards,
Ector

Messages.Author: Kevin Walsh
Messages.Body:
Fred Scott wrote:
> Sometimes you get one or two mondo bleeders, and then TM is better, all
> things considered - including your point about giving your prey a bleed
> to occupy his resources.

Well, let's look at the two scenarios presented. Assume that I can't
beat whatever stealth I'm bled with, and that I will be bled by either
two Vampires for 5, or 5 Vampires for 2. I have 2 cards which are
either Telepathic Counter or Telepathic Misdirection, an untapped
Vampires with AUS and a Wake in hand.

With two TCs, I take 6 pool either way, at the cost of zero blood.

With one TC and one TM, I take 3 pool in the first scenario, and 6 in
the second. This costs me one blood and I still have my Wake. In the
first scenario, my prey is bled for 5, and in the second, he is bled
for 2.

With two TMs, then in the first scenario, I get bled for nothing, and
my prey is bled for 10. In the second, I get bled for 6, and my prey
for 4. This costs me 2 blood and my Wake.

Now clearly, in the first scenario, investing entirely in TMs is the
way to go. In the second scenario, two TCs isn't the way to go, and
arguments can be made on both sides of the question as to whether to go
with two TMs, or one TC and one TM. So TM is looking better, right?

Well, how about scenario 3? I will be bled by 4 guys for 1, who will
not be bleeding with stealth, but will tear my head off if I block. If
I bounce them to my prey, he can block with no negative consequences.
At worst, they will strike for hands, and it's quite possible they'll
do some Maneuver/Dodge deal, or my prey will block and untap with
Majesty. In this situation, reducing the first two bleeds and taking
the next 2 on the chin seems like the best option to me. Using TMs
costs me blood, which I will need on my Vampires in order to prevent
them from going into torpor or for pulling them out of torpor if this
is some kind of Disarm deck. And unless my prey is really on the ropes,
spending 1 blood to do 1 pool damage is not likely to be a great
investment, since my own offence probably has greater returns. Also, if
I'm on the ropes, and Tension isn't in play, then with two TCs I can
reduce two bleeds, and block the other two.

Kevin Walsh

finals and get ready for a snorefest.

Messages.Author: Chris Berger

pd...@lightlink.com wrote:

>
> Telepathic Counter is clearly inferior to Telepathic Misdirection, in
> terms of efficient bleed defense.
>

I won't go as far as the other poster, since I respect you, Peter
(well, at least to some degree... =P ;) ), but I think this
statement is just plain false. First off, weenie bleed is, depending
on metagame, often more scary than bazooka bleed. TC is way better
against weenie bleed. In addition, bounce is most effective when you
attempt to block, because when they stealth past, you suddenly have a
stealth bleed against your opponent. (I'm not saying, it's only useful
when you attempt to block, but generally more so.) When you attempt to
block, you run the risk of a) cycling your opponent's hand, or b)
actually succeeding in your block, which if you have a bounce in your
hand, is often not what you really wanted. When you bounce without
blocking, most of the advantage of bounce over TC is lost, since your
prey just blocks. If he has plenty of untap, or the responsible
bleeder Changes Target, then he has lost little.

Telepathic Counter, on the other hand, denies your predator the ability
to cycle. Even in the case where you bounce without blocking, your
predator usually has the choice of stealthing past your prey (good for
you, but may also be good for him), or cycling combat cards. With TC,
you don't tap a vamp, you don't spend a blood, and you don't give him
the opportunity to cycle anything but bleed mods.

As such, TC over TM is a strongly meta-game dependent variable, as well
as being based on your deck having large vamps versus small vamps
(large vamps, IME, tend to prefer TM, small vamps prefer TC). And then
there's the small bonus that TC helps with withdrawing, if you end up
wanting/needing to do that.

>Telepathic Counter, on the other hand, denies your predator the ability
>to cycle. Even in the case where you bounce without blocking, your
>predator usually has the choice of stealthing past your prey (good for
>you, but may also be good for him), or cycling combat cards. With TC,
>you don't tap a vamp, you don't spend a blood, and you don't give him
>the opportunity to cycle anything but bleed mods.

But, at the same time, while your predator cycles against your prey,
you've got your prey having to work out how he can afford to take the
bleed, or block it - forcing him to "waste" an untapped minion, or a
wake, or whatever.

This isn't insignificant, because it can disrupt the plans of your prey,
without him having a chance to untap and regroup before you get your
turn to come in and bleed him, or do whatever it is that he might have
been blocking before. So it defends you AND can cause him problems.

In the general case, this is much better for you because it's defence
and helps your offence.

Fred Scott wrote:

> point is just that lots of defense is too rewarding, based on the

I think you are right about this. That being said, I don't think giving
non Ausepx disciplines access to viable bleed reduction (i.e. a cards
that let non Auspex disciplines reduce bleeds by 2 at superior, that
are low opportunity cost and flexible) would actually increase the
amount of defense in play.

Currently, every deck built has to answer the question "How is this
deck going to deal with a significant bleed predator". Always. Or it
isn't a viable deck. Which means that all decks are built with some
sort of bleed defense. Which might be bounce (and really, more often
than not, it is). Or might be intercept. Or might be bloat. Or might be
outrace. Decks that can't do *one* of these things are, from the
inception, inviable. And a great deal of the time, the answer is "I use
bounce, either 'cause I have AUS, or I have dom, or 'cause I bolt one
of those things on to my deck". I can't think of how many decks I have
built that look like "5 of an important Superstar and then 7 dom
weenies" or "5 of an important Superstar, and then 7 AUS weenies".
Really, it is a lot.

Introducing reasonable bleed reduction to non Auspex disciplines
(again, my best yet possibly flawed example is an Obfuscate
mod/reaction card that says +1 stealth/reduce a bleed by 2) would not,
for my money, make the game any more defensive that it currently is. It
would just mean that all those decks that have fringe dominate just for
the 8 deflections, or all those decks that are built to include AUS,
just for the Telepathic Misdirections, would get to avoid that kind of
kludgey (but incredibly common) magic defense option.

-Peter

Messages.Author: Orpheus
Messages.Body:
> Oh, and you don't have to have a deck with "regularly multiple untapped
> minions" to properly use TC. You get a TC, leave a 5-cap with AUS
> untapped.

And reduce a bleed by 2.

> Or have a hand full of TC's, leave 2 minions untapped, and
> watch the bleeder waste his actions. And you reshuffle your hand.

And reduce a few bleeds by 2.

As already said, it IS good. But not nearly as good as sending 1 or 2 bleeds
your prey's way, or wherever else you want to deal it ! Let's not forget
that redirecting can also be dealt, while reducing can only be dealt in the
case of the weak Folderol.

And I know this thread is about Auspex, but let's not forget that the
Ultimate Boucne Card, Deflection, doesn't even tap you at superior.

> And,
> as far as bleeding for 3+ goes, it's irresponsible and risky, and no
> good bleeder is ever going to go over 3, because of AI, deflections,
> misdirections, and such.

THAT is the most false and irrelevant statement I ever read on this
newsgroup, no offense intended mate. Because :

1) there are ways to know if your prey plays AI or not (Monocle : "Do you
play AI in this deck ?" ; relevations sup etc)

2) A number of these tactics can also be used to bleed more "responsibly"
and take your Intercept, TC, TM, Deflections, whatever, from your hand, so
you know it's safe to bleed for a lot.

3) Most of the decks using Intercept or Bounce don't bother to also include
AI (they just don't have the space or use for it), so I'm more cautious
about not bleeding too strongly a deck without bleed defense (or, say, just
a bunch of 2nd Trads).

4) There are moments when you can be perfectly sure that your prey can't
play AI : when she already played an OOT Master ; and this happens quite
often, with Sudden and Direct and what-have-you (played Life Boon, uh ? Now
PAY !!).

5) Many players, including very good players, consider that being bounced
isn't that bad because it hurts their "next prey" or, at the very worst,
takes a player from the table (that may be a good reasoning or not depending
on the table, I'm just saying that it is widely spread) ; many players also
think that a BIG bleed is worth risking the AI. I wouldn't do it with a big
vamp (some do...) but Gloria Giovanni bleeding for 6 is definitely worth it.
Oh, and she can be Possessed back too, necromantics are marvelous ain't they
? ;-)

> I really don't remember the last time I've seen
> a good bleeder going over 3 in my surrounding. Those kind of bleeds end
> up at seriously fuck up places around the table, or get the bleeding
> minion burned.

Not in my competitive experience. I also recall the finals at Heidelberg
(not sure if it was the EC or the day before) where there was a "I bleed the
hell out of you with Inner Circles" deck. It made it to the finals, that
could mean something. It's not the only time this happens either.

> Or generate so much hate from usually
> no-bleed-defense-combat's that they're happy to go cross table torn
> signpost-grapple-blur-agg burn them.

Maybe in friendly games, or in light competitive environments. In
tournaments where every deck is dangerous, a totally irresponsible deck
might make unwanted enemies, but a good "big bleeds" deck will be just as
dangerous as another deck. Of course if it has no way of dealing and is too
offensive, good players will kill it with crosstable votes, but that isn't
just because he can bleed hard.

> Holding 6 TC's in your deck is the
> best thing you can do with an auspex deck, because TC is NEVER, and i
> mean NEVER a dead card.

Another false statement. It is never a dead card if your prey bleeds. If
it's a voter or a rusher your hand will jam. Whereas TM is seldom a dead
card, because you can try to intercept with it too so it can help against
Ventrue Old School, +1 stealth rushes on your Famed vamp, etc. And in the
endgame you'll always find a way to cycle it, if it's more important to you
than the blood cost.

Being able to really reduce everything that comes your way (or enough to be
comparable to a bounce) will require a LOT of TCs, that will totally jam
your hand if no bleeds come your way.

But I get your meaning that TC is never dead against bleeds. Sure. It still
makes it a poor choice most of the times compared to bounce cards, for
reasons already stated all over this thread by Peter, James et al.

> Presuming you can play, though, and I can
> understand that can be tough. It saves you exactly 2/5 of your 30 pool,
> if used correctly. I consider that to be quite much, don't know about you.

I often play with quite a few deflections. I can't count the number of times
when my pred killed my first prey for me. A bounce will save ALL your pool.
As James mentionned, even redirecting bleeds for 2 (let's say Palla or
Nightmare bleeds ?) has many uses. All this with just one card per bleed,
while even the single Govern the Unaligned will either require 2 TC from you
or bleed you for one anyway (and pleaaaaase don't tell me nobody plays
Govern or an equivalent in your playgroup !).

So, given all this, and more (I just won't repeat all the sensible arguments
already stated), I really don't see how TC can be considered half as good as
bounce _in most cases_ (I did try a few Bartholomew decks with bleed
reductions when he came out, it sure was fun but under-optimized lol).
--

Orpheus

I'm dead serious ! Well, mostly dead...

Messages.Author: Kevin Walsh
Messages.Body:
Fred Scott wrote:
> Same as the last guy: cook up specific scenarios and present them as if
> they accurately demonstrate the relative value of the two cards when they
> don't.

I was using the same scenarios previously presented, and adding a third
for the sake of balance. Because, in fact, I don't think TC is as bad
as Peter has been making it out to be, or Deflection/Misdirection as
good. Often, I find myself bouncing bleeds for 1 at 1 blood per pop
just to get the damn cards out of my hand. This depends on how combat
heavy the metagame is, of course. But even in a combat heavy metagame,
you do need to plan for the occasional big bleeder.

For one thing, I don't think you're paying as much attention to
> Telepathic Counter not tapping the defender as you should. For
> instance, I didn't see you give any mouth time to the point that
> playing two Telepathic Misdirections in the same turn requires that you
> leave two vampires untapped or have a Wake as well.

I'm pretty sure I pointed out in the case of each scenario whether the
Wake was used or not.

Or that reducing
> the bleed leaves you untapped to simply block another guy eventually.
> In my experience, it's much more common to be bled by four guys for one
> at no stealth who will NOT tear your head off if you block than the way
> you proposed it.

If I can block my predator easily without serious consequences, I
probably don't need reduction or bounce. 2-3 pool loss a turn is
annoying, and not a good thing by any means, but a competently built
deck should be able to deal with it. I'm not saying it doesn't happen
(I do it frequently myself when I get Master-jammed with a combat
deck), but if this was the only thing anyone had to fear, then bleed
defence beyond Wakes wouldn't be necessary.

Of course, in that situation, TC isn't the best passive defence.
Ecstasy is. And we all know that Ecstasy is pants, not least because
SER is so much more expensive than AUS.

Kevin Walsh

Messages.Author: pd...@lightlink.com
Messages.Body:
pd...@lightlink.com wrote:
> This might be a horrible idea. But maybe not. And maybe the key is to
> do away with the idea that only Auspex gets good bleed reduction.

For the sake of illustrating this idea, here are some cards off the top
of my head that I think might be viable. Not necessarily the best of
ideas, but the kinda thing I'm talking about:

Shroud Resources
Obfuscate
Action Mod/Reaction
obf: +1 stealth
OBF: Reduce a bleed you are taking by 2.

Forced Defense
Fortitude
Combat/Reaction
for: Prevent 1 damage
FOR: Reduce a bleed you are taking by 2.

Cut Them Off At The Pass!
Celerity
Combat/Reaction
cel: Manuver or Press
CEL: Reduce a bleed you are taking by 2.

Insect Swarm
Animalism
Combat/Reaction
ani: Strike: 1R with optional manuver.
ANI: Reduce a bleed you are taking by 2.

And whatever. Not all disciplines would need this kind of card. Amd
these are all possibly stronger than they need to be (or maybe not).
The Obfuscate one, for instance, would probably be overpowered in S+B
decks (as it provides easily cycled stealth for when your prey declines
to try and block you), so that example is probably one that would need
to be something else. The combat/reaction examples are probably less
easily cycled, as you need to get into combat to use them for the
inferior version (i.e. you need to Rush someone, someone needs to block
you or you need to block someone, and if you can block them, you
probably don't need to reduce their bleeds anyway; this being said,
giving this sort of ability to combat decks means that they'll less
often be in a spot where they have to agressively back Rush, which
helps maintain table balance), but this is the kind of thing I am
proposing.

White Wolf, please feel free to take these ideas and run with them. I
claim no possession over them :-)

-Peter

Messages.Author: Nosferatu_3
Messages.Body:
ira...@gmail.com wrote:
> > One thing that I'd like to
> > see are more ways of getting around intercept as a means of pushing actions
> > through. I see too many viable deck archetypes that place such a heavy
> > reliance on intercept that it can be difficult to effect ANY kind of offense
> > against them.
>
> Doesn't that already exist in the form of block fails, better combat,
> or a lot of stealth? If you have a problem with intercept walls, play
> a deck that takes only 0 stealth actions and they'll jam on intercept.
>
> Nonetheless, I agree with you that timeouts are no fun, and playing
> against decks that are intentionally designed without much forward
> pressure isn't fun, either. I don't see that as much a flaw in card
> design, but the deck building choices of some people.
>
> Ira

I have to agree that there a ton of ways around intercept walls. Some
are much better than others. No Secrets has the potential to create
some seriously mean walls. The big trump to intercept heavy decks is
combat. I myself often play wallish decks at tournaments because of the
low frequency of combat. I think that combat (good combat) is often the
missing link in the balance equation because it is so rare at
tournaments. I don't have to sneak past a minion that I can
burn/torporize. Combat is not a very direct means of ousting, however,
and I'm sure why it is not seen more at big-time tournaments.

I find myself often frustrated with my own decks. Most of my defensive
decks really suffer from the time-out issue. At the same time, in the
last 18 months or so, I have been seated next to many aggressive
predators that would have quickly ousted a non-defensive deck. At the
same time, I don't enjoy playing sneak-bleed. I also have had some ugly
experiences with speedy decks, as I cripple and oust my first prey,
only to get a second prey I can't get through due to their build-up of
permanents that my first prey couldn't stop because of my pressure.
Perhaps I am just bringing the wrong deck for a given metagame, but no
matter how I jump, it always seems to serve another at my tables.

Messages.Author: pd...@lightlink.com
Messages.Body:
I wrote:
> As an aside, 260, as a point of data, illustrates nothing at all. We
> don't know how many decks those are in (10? 50? 100? 300?), or how many
> Telepathic Misdirections are in decks as a comparison. Maybe I'll make
> that point of data into something useful.

Clearly, I should be doing something useful with my time, but instead,
I'm doing this.

Going back to the TWDA, here is what I found, again. My sample is all
the TWDs in the archive back through Origins 2004, which is roughly 2
full years of tournament winning decks. Counting them, the sample size
is 223 decks (it might be a couple more or a couple less, as I counted
by eye rather than doing it with a computer, so we'll give it a margin
of error of +/-3 decks :-)

As noted before:

-Telepathic Misdirection is used in 72 of 223 decks (32%)
-Telepathic Counter is used in 17 of 223 decks (8%)

-There are 336 copies of Telepathic Misdirection in those 72 decks (4.7
per deck)
-There are 80 copies of Telepathic Counter in those 17 decks (4.8 per
deck)

So when folks use Telepathic Counter, they are using slightly more of
them per deck than Telepathic Misdirection ('cause they are less
efficient?). I found multiple decks that included 8-12 Telepathic
Misdirections. I found 1 deck that included 16 Telepathic Counters.

Looking for Deflection, I found:

-Deflection is used in 80 of 223 decks (36%)

I didn't count the individual number of Deflections. I also looked for
My Enemy's Enemy, which didn't show up much (once in 223 decks?), and
it is hard to find as people tend spell it differently, but the
occurance of Folderol is probably roughly equivelant to My Enemy's
Enemy, so we'll ignore those. Redirection also only shows up once or
twice in 223 decks, so we'll ignore that, too.

Realizing that some of the decks using Deflection are also using
Telepathic Misdirection, and that some of (well, most of, really--maybe
3 or 4 of the 17 decks using Telepathic Counter are not also using
Telepathic Misdirection) the decks using Telepathic Misdirection are
also using Telepathic Counter, so there is some level of error in the
following numbers (but probably not enough to really be significant):

68% of the decks in the sample use bleed bounce.
8% of the decks in the sample use bleed reduction.

I think that is reasonable evidence that people consider bleed bounce
to be significantly more useful than bleed reduction, given the choice.

-Peter

worth doing in the first place. CCG design ultimately doesn't worry
about rewarding all cleverness equally and can't. All it can do
is try to make the game as fun as possible by balancing as many
paths to victory as possible (thus facilitating diversity) and
making the ultimate character of the game fun to play (by, for
instance, avoiding heavy arbitrary luck components to play). It
is the latter point that makes me want to see the game rebalanced
towards more offense. I don't see the game having nearly as much
problem with overly offensive decks making games too fast and
arbitrary as I see it having problems with static, boring,
endless or timeout games in which deadlocks are never broken.
(And, just to rehash a clarification, I'm looking at finals
games in particular as I say that.)

> I'm all for finals finishing, but I have to say that all of the finals
> I've ever seen time out didn't do so because of negotiation.

I agree. But the fact that negotiations are effective enough that
they can often effortlessly block players trying to push the
game forward is exactly part of the problem. That, to me, is
a sign that the game is too defensive in nature. You complain
about lack of player interaction when offense is too effective.
This is the flip side caused by too much player interaction.
When players have so much ability to block other players'
progress, the game naturally goes nowhere because the only
thing all players can agree on is the point that no other
player should be allowed to win. There has to be some solution
to that and the solution is to limit the amount of power the
table has in terms of stopping any one player from getting
an oust.

Fred

> Realizing that some of the decks using Deflection are also using
> Telepathic Misdirection, and that some of (well, most of, really--maybe
> 3 or 4 of the 17 decks using Telepathic Counter are not also using
> Telepathic Misdirection) the decks using Telepathic Misdirection are
> also using Telepathic Counter, so there is some level of error in the
> following numbers (but probably not enough to really be significant):
>
> 68% of the decks in the sample use bleed bounce.
> 8% of the decks in the sample use bleed reduction.
>
> I think that is reasonable evidence that people consider bleed bounce
> to be significantly more useful than bleed reduction, given the choice.

Not exactly, no.

It means that the people who actually WIN tournaments do it lots more often
with bleed bounce than bleed reduction. It is actually even more significant
: even if lots of players chose the reduction way, they didn't win with it.
And if we're talking choices, these were done by players who know what's
needed to win tournaments. It doesn't matter which comes first - the choice
by good players or the winning because of good choice - but I think it
illustrates your point pretty well and I can't agree more, from my
experience at playing with or without Bounce (I'm pretty much unable to win
without it, maybe some day I will).

This being said, I also agree with you that bleed reduction could be nice
for anyone who can't redirect, on the condition that it's either possible to
reduce a big bleed consequently or that the card has a very good
second-option cycling possibility.

--
Orpheus

Messages.Author: Appolonius
Messages.Body:
I may be wrong here, and no doubt someone will correct me if I am. But I
believe the original motivation of this thread was to propose the
introduction of more widespread and usable bleed reduction cards as a
means of improving bleed defence for non-bounce clans, without the
perceived "homogenising" effect that introducing disciplineless bleed
bounce would have.

So it's interesting to see in some parts of the thread people have been
bending over backwards to show that Telepathic Counter (a "reduce by
two" card) is markedly inferior to Telepathic Misdirection (a bounce
card) in most situations (which I agree with). Yet those same people
elsewhere advocate that giving non-bounce disciplines "reduce by 2"
cards rather than (disciplineless) bounce cards will be adequate to
bridge the bleed defence gap. Isn't there some hint of a contradiction here?

I'm not saying the whole concept sucks - I think the "(inf) <useful
effect> / (SUP) Reduce by 2" cards are a nice idea and would definitely
see some play. But they will not level the playing field as much as
introducing disciplineless bounce would. Auspex decks currently tend to
go for TM over TC, and in the same way I predict non-bounce decks that
currently jam a "bounce module" into their crypt would choose to
continue to do so, rather than use these new cards.

I still think we need disciplineless bounce.

Appolonius.

It might. It would probably depend on the deck. You'd have to leave guys
untapped (or play lots of Wakes) to benefit much from this. Auspex decks
(the ones that use bleed reduction now) don't have much trouble with that
because they're typically already defense-oriented decks that like to leave
multiple vamps untapped in the first place. Non-Auspex decks may very well
find these non-Auspex bleed-reduction reactions to have a much greater cost
for them to use effectively, because they have to leave someone with the
superior discipline untapped to play them, or else take up even more
cardslots with a bunch of Wakes. This is also one of the reasons that
people crowbar Dominate into their decks rather than Telepathic Counters, of
course: you can Deflect with inferior Dominate, and it's less card-intensive
than Telepathic Counters to do so (because the net effect of each played
Deflection is, on average, higher than that for TC).

> build would get to avoid that particularly klunky defense angle.

I think Frank Moeller also has a good point on what disciplines ought to be
considered for these kinds of cards, and in what way the cards should work.
You don't really want to give weenie decks better defenses with these
things; I kind of think there should either be a capacity restriction on the
bleed-reduction superior (e.g. requires a vampire with capacity above 4) or,
as Frank suggested, make 'em dual-discipline (though I don't entirely like
that solution since it frequently ties down each particular bleed-reduction
card to a specific clan).

Plus, they probably shouldn't go into disciplines (at least without capacity
restrictions or something) that are already incredibly great disciplines on
their own. Obfuscate, for example, no matter how nice it would be for the
Nosferatu and Setites. :-)

Josh

disciplines

are very major and large tournaments obviously but the number

explains why Continental Championships buck the trend of lesser

I can't see how that's an issue. If the finals are full of defensive
decks (granted you think that's a questionable assumption but for
purposes of argument...), then it doesn't matter how you want to
look at it. The problem is that, in the end, the finals are full
of defensive decks. In fact, I think the above question - if I
understand it correctly - is a comparison between identical quantities.
Good players choose good decks that allow them to win and make it to
the finals. If I saw good players choosing offensive-oriented decks
and making it to the finals, then I wouldn't see timed-out finals
and I wouldn't be worrying about this issue.

> The game isn't necessarily lacking in

> doesn't mean they're doing so because defensive decks are necessarily

Of course it does - otherwise good players wouldn't choose them. In

> already. More pool-damaging options for the wackier disciplines, maybe?

> powerful cards, for instance.

Something like that. The thing I like best is the idea of more effective
ways to bypass intercept so make it risky to depend on intercept as much
as players seem to. I'm not sure that will work and I think it would
need to exist only in specialized discipline(s) because my aim is
certainly not to obsolesce intercept. It's just to discourage its use
a bit and encourage a general shift towards offense. Having a couple
more really viable archetypes that don't care about intercept (and not
just because of superior combat abilities) seems like just the thing
to me.

> Is rewarding things which are wacky routes to victory what you're
> referring to about when you talk about more offensive options, then? If
> so, I'm all in favor.

Sort of, kind of. The word "wacky" kind of bothers me because too often,
wack decks are interesting and clever but for various reasons don't turn
out to be tournament quality. But, yea. The aim is to create new
archetypes with new strengths and new weaknesses, not to buck up
stealth bleed or weeny bleed.

>> CCG design ultimately doesn't worry
>> about rewarding all cleverness equally and can't. All it can do
>> is try to make the game as fun as possible by balancing as many
>> paths to victory as possible (thus facilitating diversity)
>
> The problem with this is that in V:TES, there are only so many delivery
> systems. And since the most unusual payload in the world isn't
> effective at all without a good delivery system, there doesn't seem to
> be a good way to introduce new offensive options without dramatically
> changing the character of the game (and I'm talking about much bigger
> changes than, like, mortals in the crypt, and look at the responses to
> that). So there can't be all that much diversity without some pretty
> huge alterations, seems like.

Well, yea. The way I think about it is that the objective is to balance
different archetypes. And there's just a limit to how many can be
balanced at any given time. I'm sure the job has elements of patting
your head and rubbing your tummy as it is. Still, you can't make an
omelet without breaking a few eggs. And my perception of the current
situation bothers me - assuming it's accurate.

>> and making the ultimate character of the game fun to play (by, for
>> instance, avoiding heavy arbitrary luck components to play). It
>> is the latter point that makes me want to see the game rebalanced
>> towards more offense.
>
> That doesn't make sense to me. If everyone's deck is heavier on offense
> than defense, you're introducing more randomness into the game, since
> you're basically playing paper/rock/scissors at that point - will my
> mostly aggressive deck's one defensive answer work against my
> predator's mostly aggressive deck?

Well, again, is there *enough* randomness in the game currently, in
this sense? I mean, I'd hate to be perceived as advocating more
dumb luck into the game but right now it bothers me that the deckbuilding/
metagaming aspects of Jyhad - which have been a bit of whipping boy
amongst the elite discussing the game in forums like this newsgroup -
have gotten short shrift over the years. Everybody hates the idea
that if they build a rock deck and they sit down next to a guy with a
paper deck that they'll get waxed and there'll be nothing they can do
about it. But shouldn't astute choices on a metagame level be
rewarded, too? Right now, the above problem doesn't scare me,
because I don't think a limited shift would make things all that
bad in the sense of what you've described above. I think we can
stand a bit of movement in that direction as long is doesn't go
too far.

> I don't think I made my point very clearly, then. I'm trying to avoid
> IME's here, but it seems to me that most finals that time out do so due
> to vote decks, not wall decks. More specifically, finals time out
> because people won't shut the hell up.

I agree with your assessment of vote decks vs. wall decks. Let me
stress, it's not really that I've seen a huge influx of wall decks
in finals causing the problem. Yes, talk is a big part of the
problem though it's not only vote decks that are doing that. It's
negotiation in general, AFAICS. This includes negotiation over
intercepting actions, people Eagle Sighting cross table, and other
forms of cross-table interference to stop someone else from
accomplishing something. Someone once described to me the reason
crab buckets need no tops: because if a crab gets far enough up the
side of the crab bucket to be a threat to climb out, the other
crabs pull him back down into the bucket. Large tournament finals
look too much like crab buckets to me. I'd like to give tennis
shoes to the crabs so someone can have a chance of getting over
the top.

Fred

Appolonius wrote:
> OK. But haven't you shown in the TC vs TM discussion that such bleed
> reduction is, in fact, not a viable alternative (to bounce)?

When you have access to both bounce and reduction, the likelyhood of
reduction being a viable alternative is very small.

That being said, when you don't have access to bounce, reduction is a
vastly superior option to no bounce.

The discussion about TC being inferior to TM is meant to illustrate the
redundancy of bleed defense in Auspex (which has both) and refute the
folks who are saying "Are you insane? Bleed reduction is th best bleed
defense out there!", which it clearly is not. But bleed reduction is
certainly better than not bleed reduction. And bleed reduction is
certainly better than not bounce.

Currently, plenty of clans have no access to bleed bounce (Nosferatu,
Brujah, Gangrel, Settites, Ravanos, Assamites, Ishtari, Akunanse,
Guhuri, most of the anti-clans of the above, lots of the bloodlines)
without grafting Auspex or Dominate into a crypt. Which happens a lot,
as bounce is such a good, efficient defense, to that point that while
grafting it onto a crypt is klunky, it is usually worth it for the 8-10
deflections that end up in the deck. If these clans had access to
viable bleed reduction from in clan disciplines, they would have other
options for defense that they currently don't have. And usually are
covered by grafiting dominate into the crypt. Perhaps if in clan
disciplines provided bleed reduction (that was actually useful bleed
reduction--not highly conditional, difficult to cycle, reduction for 1
cards), the "graft dominate" plan wouldn't happen so much.

-Peter

> can also play Telepathic Misdirection, and as bleed bounce is *so* much
> better than bleed reduction, Telepathic Counter (and as such, bleed
> reduction as a general defense) mostly gets left by the wayside.

I often prefer Telepathic Counter to Telepathic Misdirection. I enjoy one
of the classic defenses against sneak/bleed (or bruise/bleed,) which is
not to block, thus choking your predator's hand with stealth (combat)
cards. Reducing the bleed works with this, but bouncing the bleed lets
her collaborate with your prey to cycle out of these cards in whatever way
best suits them.

Other benefits of TC are that it's free, it leaves you untapped, and it's
still useable when the game gets down to two players. It can also keep
your predator from getting the Edge. I still like TM for its flexibility
-- intercept OR bleed bounce -- but I don't think it's that much better
than TC. This may just be a matter of playstyle, though.

Some of the new reducers are interesting, but I still think TC is the
king. I'd love it if they made another free, non-tapping, reduce-by-2
reaction card.

There is some inherent math to the Telepathic Counter versus Telepathic
Misdirection case, though.

Against a bleed of 1:

TC costs: 1 card, must have minion with at least [aus] untapped or Woken
TC yields: 1 pool saved to you

TM costs: 1 card, 1 blood, must have minion with [AUS] untapped or Woken,
taps that minion
TM yields: 1 pool saved to you, 1 pool lost by your prey (or he/she must do
something about it)

Against a bleed of 2:

TC costs: 1 card, must have minion with [AUS] untapped or Woken
TC yields: 2 pool saved to you

TM costs: 1 card, 1 blood, must have minion with [AUS] untapped or Woken,
taps that minion
TM yields: 2 pool saved to you, 2 pool lost by your prey (unless he/she does
something)

Against a bleed of 3:

TC costs: 1 card, must have minion with [AUS] untapped or Woken
TC yields: 2 pool saved to you

TM costs: 1 card, 1 blood, must have minion with [AUS] untapped or Woken,
taps that minion
TM yields: 3 pool saved to you, 3 pool lost by your prey (unless he/she does
something)

The benefits of TM vs TC continue to increase as the bleed amount goes up,
of course.

Notice that TM's 'net swing in pool' for you versus your prey goes from 2
for a bleed of 1, to 4 for a bleed of 2, 6 for a bleed of 3, etc. TC gives
you a net swing of 1 for a bleed of 1, 2 for a bleed of 2, 2 for a bleed of
3, and remains 2 at all higher bleed levels.

This is the math behind why Telepathic Misdirection is more popular in
tournament decks than Telepathic Counter. It is more card efficient and has
a greater effect in hurting your prey at the same time it helps you.
Despite the blood cost, it is an inherently stronger card.

Very possibly you already know this math. But your argument that TC vs TM
is a strictly metagame/strategy-dependent choice seems to rest on there
being no demonstrable difference in the magnitude of the cards' effects.
There is.

Josh

Really? I think it's extremely obvious.

Consider:
Redirection (sup) vs Deflection (sup). Same effect except the Deflection
does not tap you, and costs a(n extra) blood.

Deflection (inf) vs Deflection (sup). Same effect except the superior
does not tap you, but requires an extra discipline level (= effect is
"one blood" more powerful).

Ditto Claiming the Body (san), ditto Shell Game (san), ditto Siren's
Lure (mel) (in each case the superior taps one fewer of your minions
than the inferior).

Or, as in Josh's example: A generic minion bleeds you cardlessly with no
modifiers. You do not wish to tap a blocker. The cost to you: 1 pool.

Clearly, not tapping when an effect would normally tap you is worth 1
blood or pool.

I'm also surprised to see claims that mathematical analysis of cards
"has 0 impact" and "should be taken with a large grain of salt". Games
_are_ maths, and this one is no exception.

Appolonius.

> course, rules of thumb are very personal, play-style and metagame
> dependent
> so we're back to non-comparibility.

The baseline concept of "1 action equals 1 bleed or pool" is pretty solid in
VTES, I think. I know! Cards can change that! But it is the basic math of
the game: you have 30 pool, your vampires can bleed for 1 cardlessly, they
strike for 1 in combat, hunt for 1, etc.

If you are untapped and tap to block a bleed, it saves you a pool (usually
at the cost of a blood). If you are untapped and *don't* tap to block this
bleed, instead staying untapped to block the next one, it usually saves you
a pool (as a starting point, again, cards can change that).

I think that's a pretty good reason for giving tapping a "base cost" of 1
pool. Again, cards can change that... but then, you might have Wakes! The
point of this kind of basic analysis is to look at the particular costs and
effects of these cards in the most basic case.

>> If cards can't be analyzed logically, why not just write new cards with a
>> random-text generator? No one will be able to show the difference,
>> right?
>
> That's a false dichotomy. Cards frequently can't be analyzed logically,
> if only for reasons of unfathomable complexity in two player games.
> In multiplayer games, player personality/philosophy issues make can it
> totally impossible.

That's not true at all. The *cards* can still be analyzed logically. Their
*effect on the game* may not be logically deducible, if we're going to
assume that players don't act rationally. (I would say there is certainly
quite a bit of anecdotal evidence in favor of that assumption. :-)

Yeah, it's possible for the ultimate effects even of the cards themselves to
be too complex to calculate, if there are a lot of interactions that you
need to take account of to do so. But people model things in the real world
all the time by looking at only the most significant interactions and
ignoring the others.

> This doesn't make it unimportant to design cards with care and avoid
> practically useless cards, highly undercosted cards, and other problematic
> conditions. Common sense and game experience will help you avoid these.
> They just don't prove anything in a rigid, analytical sense.

True "proof" may be impossible, but that doesn't make mathematical analysis
useless. It's a good way, in my opinion, of figuring things out beyond
appealing to common sense or anecdotal experience.

Appolonius's examples are, I think, pointing to the idea that the baseline
effect of cards in VTES typically starts at 1 pool or blood. That is,
playing a card (compared to not playing a card) is often going to give you a
"1 pool" benefit; if it costs blood, that cost may give you an additional
pool benefit; if it requires additional discipline levels, that requirement
may give you an additional pool benefit; etc.

For example:

Ascendance: costs 0 and an MPA, gains 1 pool
Computer Hacking: costs 0 and an action, gives +1 bleed (ie 2 total)
Social Charm [pre]: costs 0 and an action, gives +1 bleed
Social Charm [PRE]: costs 0 and an action, gives +1 bleed and 1 pool
Scouting Mission [dom]: costs 0 and an action, gives +1 bleed
Scouting Mission [DOM]: costs 0 and an action, gives 2 pool/transfers
Govern the Unaligned [dom]: costs 1 and an action, gives +2 bleed
Govern the Unaligned [DOM]: costs 1 and an action, gives 3 pool/transfers
Restoration [for]: costs 0 and an action, gives 2 blood
Restoration [FOR]: costs 0 and an action, gives 3 blood

Perhaps this is all accidental, but I think maybe not. :-) Also notice
here that Telepathic Counter, costing a card for each use, is right in line
with the "base" level of saving you 1 pool per card played (equal to 1
tapping per card played in my idea of baseline costs).

Then I might go further and say that the strongest card-plays are the ones
whose benefits can grow beyond 1 pool per card played. That is (IMO) why
Telepathic Misdirection (or Deflection, etc) is so impressive: the larger
the bleed amount, the bigger the savings TM can give you. That is *also*
true of Wake with Evening's Freshness - as a floating "untappedness", being
able to block a bleed of, say, 6 at the cost of a single card is a huge
payoff - which is why Wake is such a strong effect. Telepathic Counter, on
the other hand, tops out at 2 for a single card-play - not bad, but also not
the kind of "judo" effect that some cards can give you.

Josh

Of course, as of the time I wrote the above, Josh hadn't made that
contention. I find it even more tenuous and less relavent. Sometimes
the pattern holds; sometimes it fails in spectacular ways: Kiss of Ra,
Sensory Deprivation, Elder Impersonation, Torment the Soul, Psyche!,
Call of the Hungry Dead. These cards are all fantastically better
at superior than inferior.

On the other hand, once in a while there is little real additional
advantage to playing the card at superior, at least in comparison
with the inferior: Illusions of the Kindred, Disarm, Coma, Contagion
are good examples.

Sometimes, there is _no_ superior at all, thus no advantage to
possessing the discipline at superior): Army of Rats, Rampage.

Sometimes the advantage is in the currency of stealth and intercept
or some other quantity, the value of which is impossible to fix in
terms of pool and blood: Enhanced Senses, Lost In Crowds, Thrown
Sewer Lid, Night Moves, probably a lot of other cards.

Sometimes the value of advantage is just very difficult analyze
at all because the two choices are completely different: Trainer,
Truth of a Thousand Lies, My Enemy's Enemy, Nimble Feet, Pulse
of the Canaille, Terror Frenzy, things like Govern the Unaligned,
many, MANY cards really.

So this "pattern" is seen in a fair number of cards, in many more
it's not. Really, the cards vary all over the map. Superior
tends to be better than inferior and (since you can always make
inferior choice, if need be) is never worse to have. That's
about all you can say about the matter.

In any event, I don't see much relevance. I was talking about the
the value of an untapped minion. This thing is about the value
of cards; it doesn't support the actual argument really. It's just
the continuation of Josh's shorthand description of how he looks
at the game. It doesn't prove anything about anything when it
comes right down to it. It's just another rule of thumb.

Fred

Messages.Author: pd...@lightlink.com

Fred Scott wrote:
> If it's overpowered, it's overpowered
> because (some people think, anyway) it's too easy to make the weeniest
> decks full of 1-caps and 2-caps that do nothing but Computer Hack.

I don't know if it is "overpowered" in the sense of "it makes you win
too much", as I think it clearly does not. But I certainly think that
it is "overpowered" in a design sense when compared to (as previously
mentioned) Fake Out, Lucky Blow, Boxed In, and Legwork. All of those
cards provide an effect identical to an effect provided by an inferior
discipline card (manuver, +1 hand damage, press, +1 intercept) but with
an added cost (DNR--I think Legwork might even have further increased
cost). Computer Hacking provides the same kind of effect (identical to
an inferior discipline), but without the added cost of similar
disciplinless cards. Is it game breaking? Not really, no. Yeah, it
allows you to make "all caitif computer hacking" decks, but really,
those aren't much more effective than weenie presence. But in the sense
of cost and effect, yeah, I think Computer Hacking is certainly
arguably too good.

Does it need to be fixed? Probably not. And maybe a specific exception
was made for a +1 bleed action that was not made for other effects in
the name of making the game (or clans without +bleed disciplines) more
playable, which is fine.

-Peter

>already. More pool-damaging options for the wackier disciplines, maybe?
>Arika and the Malks aren't going to care much if Quietus gets some
>powerful cards, for instance.

It's often a problem when you come up with a card idea to help
something not so good that you end up with something that helps what
is already buff. I didn't have time to read through the latest help
the fatties thread, but I'm sure that came up there.

There's a couple ways to solve that which aren't too difficult. One,
add power restricted in ways that are difficult for the best to
access. For instance, help any of the !Ventrue (individual)
disciplines and the total power curve jumps. But, give them a
noncrappy clan card [whoa, crazy talk] and maybe they wouldn't be so
outclassed by the Ventrue*. Come up with a power AUS/FOR card and you
elevate them and Harbingers. You also buff Salubri and the likes of
Omaya or Laz. But, say the card was designed in some way that it was
better with multiple similar vampires.

* I've long since stopped complaining that the !Ventrue suck as
there's enough others who could use more help, just that they are the
Ventrue are so much stronger. Still, they should get better clan
cards (that aren't vampires).

For instance:
Shared Intensity
Action
+1 stealth action.
[aus]/[for]: Put this card in the acting vampire. All other vampires
you control that possess both Auspex and Fortitude may prevent 1
damage each combat. Burn this card during your next untap phase.
[AUS]/[FOR]: As above, but the affected vampires also gain +1
intercept and an optional press each combat.

There's the list of checklist problems to go through: Does it help
weenie decks? Does it help known strong decks? Does it kill existing
decks that are interesting? Etc.

Glancing at it, I'd say the greatest problem is lack of power. Maybe
the inferior should be an optional press and the superior should be
prevent 2 damage each combat as there's a big jump between one damage
and two even if the Imbued discourage random agg. Oh well, I didn't
do *that much* design back in the day.

The other simple thing to do to prevent the best from getting better
is give others what the best already have. If Quietus had Govern and
Conditioning or Govern and Deflection or Conditioning and Deflection,
it still wouldn't be as good as Dominate and, being far less
frequently available, people would find it difficult to come up with
something better than what's already possible. So, one way to create
a new card to fill a helper role is to go through what strong
vampires/decks are already capable of and simulate for the
disenfranchised. A Necromancy Voter Cap would be ...

> In fact, it's not even a problem outside of weenie decks.

No where in my argument am I claiming it is a problem anywhere. I will
state this very clearly here:

Computer Hacking Does Not Need An Increased Cost. It Is Fine The Way It
Is. It Is Not Over Powered In The Sense Of Needing To Be Fixed. It Does
Not Create Problems. At All.

Right. Now that that is clear, I think it is a very obvious design
outlier, when compared to similar disciplinless cards. And maybe that
was a mistake that was ratified by the passage of time. Or maybe it was
a specific design decision. But still, in a game design sense, Computer
Hacking is a card that is clearly more effective than it should be.

> No it's not. What problem does is cause? It doesn't. You're comparing
> unlike quantities and expecting a pattern to hold that doesn't need
> to be there.

Go back and read my paragraph 3 up from here. The one where all the
words start with capital letters. And come back down when you are
done...

Ok. This is just like Ian Forrestal all over again. Ian Forrestal is
arguably "too powerful" in the context of how the rest of the game is
designed ('cause he is an 8 cap vampire with, effectively, 30+ points
in disciplines). I'm not restarting that argument, just using it as a
paralell. Ian Forrestal does not need to be "fixed" in any sense, as he
doesn't have really any negative impact on the game at all. Neither
does Computer Hacking. Yet still, in a design sense, it is more
powerful than it should be, compared to all other similar disciplinless
cards.

-Peter

Messages.Author: pd...@lightlink.com
Messages.Body:
Fred Scott wrote:
> OK, you don't think it's "bad" enough to need to be fixed. I don't think it's really bad at all.

I don't think Computer Hacking is bad at all. I think it is fine just
the way it is. But I also think it is important to recognize that
Computer Hacking is the exception to the "how to design disciplinless
cards" system, not the rule. Fake Out, Lucky Blow, and Arson are all
fine as they are, and see use enough to justify them existing (Legwork
and Boxed In, less so), even with their added cost. Computer Hacking is
clearly outside of that design system (i.e. it provides an effect
identical to that of a discipline card, yet has no added cost) for
reasons that are unknown (maybe an accident; maybe by design). Further
disciplinless cards should follow the general rule provided by Lucky
Blow, Fake Out, and Arson. Not Computer Hacking. Just like how Ian
Forrestal is the exception, rather than the rule, for vampire
design--it isn't actually problematic that Ian Forrestal exists, as
long as other vampires aren't built, using him as a precident (which
hasn't happened since Ian Forrestal was printed, notably).

-Peter

Fata morgana would be the poster child..... two cards, bleed for 3 at 1
stealth. That would be what we call a "Git 'er dun" down here in the
land of *REALLY* friendly family reunions.

But there are lots of little +1 bleed action mods scattered around the
disciplines. Leaving out the ones that occur in PRE, DOM, or DEM you
have:

AUS: Ancestor's Insight
VAL: Burning Touch
VIC: Changeling
CHI: Fata Morgana
Guruhi: Guruhi Are the Land, The
ABO: Predator's Mastery
SER: Revelations of Desire, Weight of the Heart (with aus), Truth of 1K
Lies (+2 bleed)

So any deck using those disciplines could feasibly run a Hack + juice
core and bleed for 3.

Then you could stretch the model a little further and encorporate
something akin to "transients padding permenants" which works so well
with intercept and combat (everything really, but that's where it's
been demonstrated over and over again). It's not so much a combo
anymore, but doing something like this:

1 Tasha, 1 J.S Simmons, 2xLaptops, 8x Computer Hacks

.... could be good. That's just 12 cards for the payload. It's not
huge and you probably want to stir it up with something else, but as
part of a two-pronged assault it looks totally reasonable. What is it
without the hacks? Just 4 prayerish cards you hope you can flow into.
And lastly there's "my crypt has +1 bleed" type of affairs.
